what_its_for: Progesterone is a natural hormone used to treat several conditions. It is most commonly used to protect the lining of the uterus in women who take estrogen therapy, to treat irregular or missed menstrual periods, to support pregnancy in women undergoing fertility treatments, and to help prevent early miscarriage. It may also be used for other hormone-related conditions as directed by your doctor.
how_to_take: Progesterone comes in different forms: capsules you swallow by mouth, vaginal capsules or suppositories you insert into the vagina, and vaginal gel. If you are taking the oral capsules (Prometrium), swallow them whole with a full glass of water. It is best to take oral capsules at bedtime because they can make you feel drowsy. If you are using a vaginal form, wash your hands before and after inserting it. Use the applicator provided if one is included. Do not eat, drink, or insert anything else into the vagina for at least 30 minutes after using the vaginal gel. Take this medication exactly as your doctor prescribed — do not take more or less than directed.
dosing: Your dose depends on why you are taking progesterone and which form you are using. Common examples include: Oral capsules for hormone therapy — often 200 mg once daily at bedtime for 12 days per month. Vaginal gel (Crinone) for fertility support — often one applicator (90 mg) once or twice daily. Vaginal suppositories (Endometrin) — often 100 mg inserted two to three times daily. Always follow the specific dosing schedule your doctor gave you, as doses vary widely between patients and conditions.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it or use it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next scheduled dose, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Do not double up or take two doses at once to make up for a missed one. If you are unsure what to do, call your doctor or pharmacist for guidance.
storage: Store oral capsules and vaginal suppositories at room temperature, between 59°F and 77°F (15°C to 25°C). Keep them away from heat, direct sunlight, and moisture. Do not store in the bathroom. Keep the vaginal gel at room temperature and do not freeze it. Keep all forms of this medication out of the reach of children and pets. Check the expiration date on the package and properly dispose of any unused or expired medication.
what_to_avoid: Avoid drinking alcohol while taking progesterone, especially oral capsules, as it can increase dizziness and drowsiness. Avoid driving, operating heavy machinery, or doing activities that require full alertness until you know how this medication affects you — oral progesterone can cause significant drowsiness. Avoid smoking, as it may increase the risk of blood clots when using hormone therapies. Do not use tampons, douches, or other vaginal products unless your doctor tells you it is okay, especially if you are using the vaginal form. Tell your doctor about all medications, vitamins, and herbal supplements you take, as some drugs like certain antifungals, antibiotics, and seizure medications can interact with progesterone.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you experience any of the following: sudden chest pain, shortness of breath, or coughing up blood (possible blood clot in the lungs); sudden severe headache, vision changes, weakness, or numbness on one side of the body (possible stroke); pain, swelling, or redness in your leg (possible blood clot); unusual vaginal bleeding or discharge; signs of an allergic reaction such as rash, hives, swelling of the face, lips, or throat, or difficulty breathing; severe dizziness or fainting; yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice); breast lumps; or symptoms of depression, mood changes, or unusual sadness. Also contact your doctor if your symptoms do not improve or if you have any concerns about side effects.
when_it_works: How quickly progesterone works depends on why you are using it. If you are using it to support a pregnancy or fertility treatment, it begins working right away to help maintain the uterine lining, but you may not notice obvious effects. If you are using it to regulate your menstrual cycle, you may see results — such as a period — within a few days after finishing a course of treatment. For hormone therapy, you may begin to feel relief from symptoms within a few weeks. Your doctor will schedule follow-up visits to check how well the medication is working for you.
special_populations: Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Progesterone is sometimes intentionally prescribed during early pregnancy to support it. However, do not use it during pregnancy unless your doctor specifically prescribed it for that purpose. It may pass into breast milk, so talk to your doctor if you are breastfeeding. Older adults: Older women using progesterone as part of hormone therapy should be aware of increased risks of blood clots, stroke, and breast cancer with long-term use. Use the lowest effective dose for the shortest time needed. Liver disease: Progesterone is processed by the liver, so if you have liver problems, tell your doctor before starting this medication. Peanut allergy: The oral capsule form (Prometrium) contains peanut oil — do NOT take it if you are allergic to peanuts. Inform your doctor immediately so an alternative form can be prescribed.
